title: Intercompany transactions: five examples explained | About Manchester
summary: A £900 sale between two subsidiaries is revenue for the seller, yet contributes no external revenue to the group. The difference lies in whose accounts you are reading. Intercompany transactions are exchanges between separate companies within a corporate group, including a parent

raw_evidence: A £900 sale between two subsidiaries is revenue for the seller, yet contributes no external revenue to the group. The difference lies in whose accounts you are reading Intercompany transactions are exchanges between separate companies within a corporate group, including a parent and subsidiary or two subsidiaries. Each records its own side of the transaction; consolidated accounts present the included companies as one economic entity. A charge These illustrative examples assume wholly owned companies included in the same consolidation and set aside tax, currency and impairment effects Company A buys stock from an external supplier for £600, then sells it to Company B for £900. A records £900 revenue and £600 cost of sales; B records £900 inventory At group level, the internal sale is eliminated from revenue. Finance teams can use financial consolidation software to support that process, working from records that identify the other company and transaction amount Suppose all the stock remains unsold to external customers at the reporting date. B’s £900 inventory includes £300 profit made inside the group. Eliminating this unrealised profit reduces group inventory to its original £600 cost and removes the internal gain from group profit

summary: Living in Manchester means accepting that rain is practically a permanent fixture on your calendar. That relentless North West damp air has an annoying habit of turning a fresh, polished morning style into a frizzy mess before you even manage to reach the tram stop. Navigating co

raw_evidence: Living in Manchester means accepting that rain is practically a permanent fixture on your calendar. That relentless North West damp air has an annoying habit of turning a fresh, polished morning style into a frizzy mess before you even manage to reach the tram stop. Navigating co Hair naturally swells when it absorbs excess moisture from humid air, causing the outer cuticle layer to lift and create instant frizz. Keeping your strands properly hydrated while you are still in the shower stops them from seeking out and soaking up that damp outdoor air later Hair is at its most fragile state when wet because the internal structural bonds temporarily stretch. Yanking a standard comb or an aggressive paddle brush through damp strands creates micro-breakage that eventually shows up as frayed split ends a few weeks down the line. Adoptin Rough towel drying destroys smooth hair texture faster than almost anything else in your routine. Vigorously rubbing your head with a heavy bath towel roughens the cuticle layer instantly and triggers immediate frizz before you even reach for a hairdryer. A much smarter approach Whenever local humidity levels spike, using heat styling tools without proper pre-styling protection almost guarantees dull, damaged ends. Layering a lightweight leave-in conditioner or a thermal spray shields your hair before you blow-dry. Plenty of beauty enthusiasts regularly Rethinking how you treat damp hair makes an incredible difference in how well your style holds up outdoors. A few small, intentional tweaks to your daily routine will keep your hair looking healthy, smooth, and effortless every day of the week

In Greater Manchester, from the terraces of Salford to the high streets of Stockport and the estates of Oldham, neighbours, schools, workplaces and local groups all play a part in helping people feel Support also needs to reach people in different ways, because no two experiences are the same. Some people find strength in a walking group, a community café or a peer support network, while others need specialist help for issues such as addiction, which can sit alongside anxiety Loneliness can affect anyone, including young adults, new parents, carers, older people and those who have recently moved to the area. Community centres, libraries, sports clubs, allotment groups and local arts projects can help people form meaningful relationships. Even small ge Greater Manchester has many diverse communities, and support should be culturally sensitive and accessible. This means providing information in different languages, recognising different family structures, and working with trusted local leaders who understand the needs of their n Stigma remains one of the biggest barriers to getting support. Communities can help by making conversations about mental health ordinary and respectful. Schools, colleges, workplaces and community groups can run awareness sessions, invite speakers with lived experience, and share It is important to use everyday language. People don’t always describe themselves as “depressed” or “anxious”; they may say they are exhausted, overwhelmed, angry, numb or unable to cope. Listening without rushing to offer solutions can make a real difference

It stands for "House in Multiple Occupation" and refers to properties where three or more unrelated people live, usually with separate bedrooms but shared facilities such as kitchens and bathrooms While HMOs are often associated with students and young professionals, they can also provide accommodation for people leaving prison, those recovering from drug or alcohol problems, and refugees Police in Salford have said they believe that the recent spate of vandalism aimed at HMOs in the area has been "racially or religiously motivated" The term HMO was formalised in the Housing Act 1985. Before then, and for many years afterwards, such properties were more commonly known as bedsits or lodging houses

raw_evidence: A groundbreaking new policing model aimed at making the Bee Network one of the safest public transport networks in the world has been launched across Greater Manchester The dedicated unit has been formed with funding from the Mayor of Greater Manchester with an Operation Vulcan-style problem-solving approach to tackling crime and anti-social behaviour, making the Bee Network one of the safest public transport networks in the world Led by Chief Superintendent Suzanne Downey, the command will effectively establish the Bee Network as GMP’s 11 th policing district, which will include over 60 new officers on the network, being supported by staff from TfGM all involved in keeping the network safe and providing g Chief Constable Sir Stephen Watson said: “TPACC represents a significant step forward in how we police and protect Greater Manchester’s transport network “By bringing policing, intelligence and transport partners closer together than ever before, we can respond more effectively to incidents, increase visibility across the network and provide even greater reassurance to passengers “We are expressly determined to tackle anti-social behaviour and to proactively deny the use of our roads, and the entire transport system, to criminals
